lead: Every file you see is a name in a directory. The name points to an inode, a numbered record that holds the file's metadata and data locations. cp, mv, rm and ln change names or inodes, so knowing which one changes decides what survives. find searches the tree by inode properties such as type, size, time and permission. These commands run daily on servers and phones: copying a project, moving a download, deleting logs, linking a config, finding old files.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the single tree and file types, and Chapter 2.2 for ls -l and viewing files.

blocks.text: A directory is a file whose data is a table of entries. Each entry is a name plus an inode number. The inode is a numbered record that holds the file type, permissions, owner, size, times, link count and data block pointers; the name is not in the inode. A file system is one mounted tree with its own set of inode numbers. The link count is the number of directory entries that point to an inode. Removing one name lowers the count; the data blocks are freed only when the count reaches 0.

items: mkdir -p /home/ravi/work/logs creates any missing parent directories and does not fail if the path already exists.
rmdir work/logs removes an empty directory only.
cd work changes the current directory of the shell; pwd prints the absolute path of that directory.
touch notes.txt creates an empty file if it does not exist, or updates its access and modification times if it does.

blocks.text: cp notes.txt backup.txt reads the source inode and writes a new inode with copied data. The two files are independent after the copy. cp -r dir1 dir2 copies a directory tree. cp -p preserves mode, ownership where permitted, and timestamps. cp -i asks before overwriting. cp -u copies only when the source is newer than the destination or the destination is missing. cp -d copies a symbolic link as a link, not as the file it points to.

mv old new inside one file system changes a directory entry: the inode number and data stay the same. Across file systems, mv must copy the data to a new inode and then remove the old name, so the inode number changes. If the destination is a directory, the file keeps its name inside that directory. Use mv -i before an overwrite you did not plan.

rm notes.txt removes one directory entry and lowers the inode link count by 1. The data survives while any other name points to that inode. rm -r dir removes a directory and its contents. rm -i asks for each file; rm -f never prompts and ignores missing names. rm -rf is fast and has no undo and no recycle bin; a wrong space or wildcard can delete a tree. Check the target with ls or find ... -print first.

sections.h3: Hard links, symbolic links and find

blocks.text: ln notes.txt hard.txt makes a hard link: a second directory entry for the same inode. The link count rises by 1. Both names read and write the same data, and the data remains until the count reaches 0. A hard link cannot cross a file system because the directory entry stores an inode number, and inode numbers are local to one file system. Most systems also forbid hard links to directories, to keep the tree acyclic.

ln -s notes.txt soft.txt makes a symbolic link. ln -s creates a new inode of type link; its data is the text of the target path. The target's link count does not change. If the target is removed, the link remains and is dangling: cat soft.txt gives “No such file or directory”. A relative target is resolved from the directory that holds the link. A symbolic link may cross file systems and may point to a directory.

find /home/ravi -type f -size +1M -mtime -7 -print searches the tree. -name '*.log' matches a name, -type f picks regular files, -size +1M is larger than 1 MB, -mtime -7 is modified in the last 7 days, -perm 644 matches permission bits, -exec cmd {} \; runs a command on each match, and -delete removes matches. Test with -print before -delete. To archive before deleting, tar -cvf backup.tar dir/ stores names and data in one file.

figure.caption: Each hard link is another name for inode 1042, so the link count goes 2, 2, 1 and the 300 bytes survive rm notes.txt. soft.txt has its own inode 2011 holding only the text notes.txt, so it dangles once that name is gone.

examples.question: /home/ravi and /home/ravi/work are on the same file system. notes.txt in /home/ravi has inode 1042 and 300 bytes. Step 1: ln notes.txt hard.txt. Step 2: ln -s notes.txt soft.txt. Step 3: rm notes.txt. (a) Give the link count of inode 1042 after each step. (b) What does cat hard.txt print after step 3, and why? (c) What does cat soft.txt print after step 3? (d) Write a find command that lists regular files under /home/ravi larger than 1 MB and modified in the last 7 days. (e) Then run mv hard.txt work/. Does the inode number change?
steps: Before step 1, notes.txt is one directory entry for inode 1042, so the link count is 1.
After step 1, hard.txt is a second entry for inode 1042. The link count becomes 1 + 1 = 2.
Step 2 creates soft.txt as a symbolic link on a new inode, 2011. Its stored data is the path text notes.txt. Inode 1042 is not linked again, so its link count stays 2.
Step 3 removes the entry notes.txt and lowers the link count of inode 1042 by 1: 2 - 1 = 1. hard.txt still points to inode 1042.
(a) The link counts after steps 1, 2 and 3 are 2, 2 and 1.
(b) cat hard.txt prints the 300 bytes of file data. hard.txt is still a name for inode 1042, and the data is freed only at link count 0.
(c) cat soft.txt fails with “No such file or directory”. The link stores the text notes.txt, and that name no longer exists, so the link is dangling.
(d) find /home/ravi -type f -size +1M -mtime -7 -print lists regular files larger than 1 MB modified in the last 7 days.
(e) mv hard.txt work/ stays inside one file system, so it only changes the directory entry. The inode number stays 1042 and the link count stays 1.
examples.answer: The link counts after steps 1, 2 and 3 are 2, 2 and 1; hard.txt still prints the data, soft.txt is dangling, and the same-file-system mv leaves the inode number unchanged.

after2 = after1
after3 = after2 - 1

traps: rm does not always free data; it removes one name. Data remains if another hard link exists, so check the link count.
rm -rf has no undo and no recycle bin; a space in the wrong place removes a different tree. Test with ls or find -print first.
A symbolic link can be dangling and still exist; a hard link cannot cross a file system because inode numbers are local to one file system.
mv across file systems copies and deletes, so the inode changes; mv inside one file system only renames the entry, so the inode stays.
find -delete acts as soon as it matches; -print is not just decoration. Run the same find with -print first.

quiz.q: What does rm file do to the inode link count?
quiz.a: It removes one directory entry and lowers the link count by 1. The data is freed when the count reaches 0.

quiz.q: Why can a hard link not cross a file system?
quiz.a: A directory entry stores an inode number, and inode numbers are unique only inside one file system. Another file system has its own inode table. A symbolic link stores a path and can cross file systems.

quiz.q: A file has link count 3. You remove one name with rm, then create a new hard link to a remaining name with ln. What is the link count now?
quiz.a: Start at 3. rm makes it 3 - 1 = 2. ln makes it 2 + 1 = 3.

quiz.q: Write a find command for regular files under /data larger than 10 MB and modified in the last 2 days.
After ln -s notes.txt soft.txt, rm notes.txt is run. Why does cat soft.txt fail while cat hard.txt works if ln notes.txt hard.txt was also run?
quiz.a: hard.txt is another directory entry for the same inode, so the data still has a name and a positive link count. soft.txt is a separate inode whose data is the path text notes.txt; that name is gone, so the symbolic link is dangling.

quiz.q: A file is moved from /home/ravi to /mnt/usb. Does its inode number change? Why?
quiz.a: Yes. These paths are on different file systems. mv must copy the data to a new inode on /mnt/usb and then remove the old name on /home.

quiz.q: What does cp -p preserve that plain cp may not?
quiz.a: It preserves mode bits, ownership where permitted, and timestamps.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems often replace cp with rsync for resumable copies and checksums. Backup scripts combine find with tar or rsync. Containers use overlay file systems, so hard links and inodes behave differently from a plain disk. Security reviews check symbolic links because a link can point outside a web root. Search next for inode, rsync, overlayfs and symlink attack.
